newsitem.title: POLAND: Pope, returning to Poland, worries over homeland.
newsitem.headline: Pope, returning to Poland, worries over homeland.

text.p: Pope John Paul ll began a nostalgic 11-day trip to Poland on Saturday, saying that while he was deeply moved to be home, he was worried about some recent changes in the country including liberalised abortion.
"Every time I return home, I am deeply touched," the 77-year-old Pontiff, who has had various health problems, told welcomers at a rainswept airport in Wroclaw, southern Poland.

"Every return to Poland is like a return under the roof of the parental home, where every little object reminds me of what is closest and dearest," said the Pope, standing with head bowed and his left arm shaking in what is believed to be a symptom of Parkinson's disease.
Speaking briefly to reporters aboard his plane the Pope seemed in good form, joking about the rain awaiting him.
But asked if he was disillusioned by some recent changes in his homeland he said: "Yes, certainly, from better to worse."
Greeting him at the airport, Poland's ex-communist President Aleksander Kwasniewski issued a plea to help build bridges rather than walls between political opponents.
Kwasniewski, who visited the Pope in April, later spoke with him privately for 20 minutes in Wroclaw's Town Hall.
The president told reporters afterwards the Pope understood Poland's opportunites but also its weaknesses and would give observations, warnings and encouragement during his trip.
"We should all accept these observations sincerely and ponder their meaning, how we can be better," Kwasniewski added.

The Pope in his arrival address congratulated Poles for economic, social and political achievements since the 1989 fall of communism and noted an infusion of optimism in the country as it went about the hard task of "learning about democracy".
Poland's economic growth is among the fastest in the former East Bloc and it is advancing towards its goals of joining Western structures including NATO and the European Union.
But passions rage over issues often linked with religion's role as campaigns start for elections due in September.
The Pope said in his address he could not hide his concern over "problems and tensions that are at times very painful".

"(These) must be resolved through a common and caring effort by all, in respect of the rights of each person, and especially the most defenceless and weak," he added in what Vatican spokesman Jaoquin Navarro-Valls said was a reference to abortion, now the topic of fierce debate in Poland.

The pro-Catholic, trade union-led Solidarity Election Action (AWS) is hoping to supplant the secularist ex-communists now in government at the parliamentary polls and its members hope the Pope's visit will help its chances.
Ex-communists in parliament have stalled a concordat treaty with the Vatican and backed a new constitution, narrowly approved in May 25 referendum, which was opposed by the Church.
Most crucially, last year the ex-communists and some other parties eased the abortion law, a move which has just been challenged by a Polish constitutional court.
Kwasniewski asked the Pope to help cool emotions.

"We Poles today need bridges bringing us together and not the building of walls which divide us," he said, quoting the Pope's own words that even complex questions could be solved by dialogue and solidarity without blurring differences of views.
Kwasniewski, now a social democrat, paid tribute to the Pope's role in the struggle that restored democracy in 1989.
"Let this be said clearly, there would have been no such change without Your Holiness and the Catholic Church in Poland," Kwasniewski said in his airport greeting statement.

As the Pope drove to Wroclaw's cathedral, crowds of tens of thousands and windows festooned with flags, portraits and flowers in Vatican and Polish colours testified to the Pope's continued great popularity among his compatriots.
He was to celebrate a mass on Sunday in Wroclaw, then travel to 11 other centres of the West and South in his seventh return home since his 1978 election.
Vatican officials say the Pope knows each visit to Poland may be his last, and the most poignant moments may be in Krakow where he was cardinal and where his parents are buried.
